title: Remove Invalid Parentheses
description: Brute force to optimized: full subset enumeration versus BFS level by level, where depth directly represents the number of parens removed.

blocks.text: Problem Summary: Given a string s containing lowercase letters and parentheses, remove the MINIMUM number of invalid parentheses so that the resulting string is valid (every open paren has a matching close paren, in the correct order). Return all possible results achieving this minimum, with no duplicates, in any order.

blocks.caption: What goes in, what comes out

{"headers":["Signal in the problem","Pattern it points to"],"rows":[["\"Minimum removals to make something valid, then ALL ways achieving that minimum\"","BFS level by level (each level = one more removal), returning the first level with any valid result"],["A validity check (balanced parentheses) applied repeatedly","A simple linear-scan counter check, reused at every level"]]}

blocks.text: The string may have unmatched parentheses (extra closes without a matching open, or extra opens never closed). Removing the fewest possible parentheses characters should produce a valid string, and every distinct way of achieving that minimum removal count should be returned.

blocks.title: Analogy: Correcting the Fewest Typos in a Balanced Expression
blocks.text: Picture proofreading a formula with occasional extra or misplaced parentheses. You want to make the fewest possible deletions to fix it, and you want every distinct minimal-deletion fix, not just one.

blocks.caption: BFS explores removing 0, then 1, then 2, ... parens, stopping at the first level with any valid result

blocks.text: Result: ["(())()", "()()()"], both reachable by removing exactly one parenthesis.

Before trying to cleverly compute which specific parens to remove, notice this is naturally a "minimum number of removals, then all ways" problem, which BFS handles cleanly: explore removing 0 characters, then 1, then 2, and so on, stopping at the very first level where at least one resulting string is valid (guaranteeing minimality) and collecting every valid string at that level.

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: BFS naturally processes states level by level, where level k represents "strings reachable by removing exactly k parenthesis characters (in some way) from the original."

Observation 2: The FIRST level containing any valid string is guaranteed to represent the MINIMUM number of removals needed, since BFS explores states in increasing order of removal count.

Observation 3: At each level, generate the next level by taking every string from the current level and, for every parenthesis character in it, producing a new string with that one character removed (skipping already-seen strings to avoid duplicate work).

Observation 4: Once a level contains at least one valid string, filter that ENTIRE level for validity and return all of them, since any string still being explored at a later level would require MORE removals than necessary.
This leads to BFS over strings, where each step removes one parenthesis character in every possible way, stopping and returning all valid strings the moment any appear at a given level.
Consider every subset of positions to remove (focusing on parenthesis characters), check which result in valid strings, and keep those with the fewest removed characters.

items: Enumerate every subset of the string's characters to keep (equivalently, every subset of parens to remove).
For each subset, check if the resulting string (keeping only the chosen characters) is valid.
Track the maximum length seen among valid results, then collect only the valid results of that maximum length (fewest removals).

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: Enumerating every subset (2^n) directly checks all possible removal combinations, guaranteed correct but wasteful.
No structure is reused between different subset checks, and non-paren characters are needlessly included in the subset enumeration.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(2^n times n), enumerating all subsets and validating each.
Space: O(2^n times n) for storing all valid results before filtering to the best length.

Limitation: this explores every possible number of removals, even far more than necessary; BFS naturally stops at the FIRST (minimum) removal count with any valid result, avoiding wasted exploration of larger removal counts.

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text:
Why full subset enumeration is wasteful: it explores every possible removal count, including many far larger than the true minimum, and only filters afterward.

The BFS insight: since BFS explores states in strictly increasing order of "number of parens removed so far," the FIRST level where any string is valid is automatically the minimum removal count, no explicit length comparison needed.

Generating the next level efficiently: only parenthesis characters need to be considered for removal (letters can never cause invalidity), and a seen-set avoids reprocessing the same intermediate string multiple times.

The core idea: BFS level by level, removing one paren at a time, stopping at the first level with any valid result and returning all valid strings from exactly that level.

BFS starting from s itself. At each level, check if any string is valid; if so, return all valid strings from that level. Otherwise, generate the next level by removing each parenthesis character (one at a time, in every position) from every string in the current level, skipping duplicates via a seen set.

blocks.caption: BFS stops at the first level containing any valid string, returning all of them (guaranteeing minimum removals)

blocks.text: BFS explores strings in strictly increasing order of how many parens have been removed to reach them. This guarantees that the first level containing ANY valid string represents the true minimum removal count, since every string still being explored at deeper levels required strictly more removals. Collecting every valid string at exactly that level, and only that level, produces every distinct minimal-removal result with no unnecessary exploration of larger removal counts.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(2^n times n) in the worst case (each level can branch, though the seen-set prunes duplicates), but in practice stops much earlier since real invalid strings usually need few removals.
Space: O(2^n times n) worst case for the seen set and level lists.

blocks.text: Remove Invalid Parentheses is a strong example of using BFS not for shortest-path-in-a-graph, but for "minimum number of edits, then all ways achieving it," since BFS explores states in order of edit count by construction.

items: Continuing to generate deeper levels even after finding valid strings at the current level (unnecessary extra work; the answer is fully determined once any level has a valid string).
Forgetting the seen-set, causing the same intermediate string to be reprocessed many times.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Case","Expected Behavior"],"rows":[["s is already valid","Returned immediately at level 0, with zero removals."],["s becomes empty before any valid string is found","Return [\"\"], as removing everything trivially satisfies validity (this is itself a valid minimal answer in that scenario)."]]}

blocks.text: Explicitly explaining "BFS here represents increasing removal count, so the first level with a hit is automatically minimal" clearly justifies why BFS (rather than DFS) is the right tool.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: If the interviewer says "find the minimum number of X, then all ways achieving it", think: BFS level by level, where level = X count, stop at first hit.

items: How would you solve this with DFS and pruning (using counts of excess "(" and ")") instead of BFS?
How would you adapt this if letters also needed some validity constraint?
Valid Parentheses, the underlying validity check reused at every BFS level.
Any "minimum edits, then all optimal results" problem, solved by BFS over edit states.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text: Both approaches share the same worst-case exponential bound, but BFS level-by-level naturally stops at the true minimum removal count without needing explicit length bookkeeping, unlike full subset enumeration.

items: Pattern: BFS over strings, where BFS depth directly represents the number of characters removed.
Core Idea: explore removing 0, then 1, then 2, ... parens; stop and return all valid strings at the first level where any exist.
Time: O(2^n times n) worst case for both approaches, though BFS stops earlier in practice.
Space: O(2^n times n) worst case for both.
Most Important Observation: BFS naturally explores states in increasing "edit count" order, making the first hit automatically minimal.
Interview Difficulty: a strong example of reusing BFS beyond graph shortest-paths, for "minimum edits" problems.
One line memory trick: BFS by removal count; first level with a valid string is the answer.
